workflows.title: Caries prevention regimen by age and risk
workflows.overview:
## 1. Decide age band

DBOH gives separate prevention regimens for four bands. Pick one, then choose general-population or higher-risk advice within it.

- **0 to 3 years**
- **3 to 6 years**
- **7 to 17 years**
- **Adults (18+)**

## 2. General-population advice for the band

### 0 to 3 years
- Brush twice daily, last thing at night plus one other time
- **Smear** of toothpaste with at least **1,000ppm** fluoride
- Parent or carer brushes
- Minimise sugar; avoid sugar at bedtime; sugar-free medicines
- Bottle: only breastmilk, formula or cooled boiled water; free-flow cup from 6 months; discourage bottle from 1 year

### 3 to 6 years
- Brush twice daily, **pea-sized** amount of at least **1,000ppm** toothpaste
- Parent or carer assists up to age 7
- **Spit, do not rinse**
- Apply **fluoride varnish 2x/year** (general population, strong recommendation)

### 7 to 17 years
- Brush twice daily with **1,350 to 1,500ppm** toothpaste
- Spit, do not rinse
- Fluoride varnish 2x/year
- Avoid tobacco and alcohol

### Adults
- Brush twice daily with **1,350 to 1,500ppm** toothpaste
- Spit, do not rinse
- Recall 3 to 24 months based on risk

## 3. Identify higher-risk patients

Giving concern includes: current or past caries, sibling caries, GA for extractions, learning or physical disability, medical compromise (e.g. diabetes), frail older people, dry-mouth-causing therapy, homelessness, hypoplastic teeth, partially erupted third molars.

## 4. Add higher-risk interventions

Layer these **on top of** the general advice for the band.

### Caries-risk children (0 to 6)
- Use **1,350 to 1,500ppm** toothpaste
- Fluoride varnish **2 or more** times per year
- Diet investigation (Eatwell Guide)
- Liaise with GP for sugar-free long-term medicines

### Caries-risk children (7 to 17)
- Fluoride varnish **2 or more** times per year
- Resin sealants on permanent teeth on eruption
- Fluoride mouthrinse **0.05% NaF (230ppm)** daily, different time from brushing, from age 8 with active caries
- **2,800ppm** toothpaste from age 10 with active caries
- **2,800 or 5,000ppm** toothpaste from age 16 with active caries
- Dietary analysis and sugar reduction

### Caries-risk adults
- Support brushing where required (carer, specialised brush, non-foaming paste)
- Fluoride varnish 2x/year
- Daily 0.05% NaF rinse for active coronal or root caries
- **2,800 or 5,000ppm** toothpaste for active coronal or root caries until stabilised
- Dietary analysis; liaise with GP for sugar-free meds

## 5. Set recall

Recall interval is risk-based, in line with NICE CG19. Shortest interval 3 months. Maximum 12 months for under-18s, 24 months for adults.

workflows.title: Choosing fluoride toothpaste strength
workflows.overview:
## 1. Establish age and risk

Toothpaste fluoride concentration is driven by **age** and **caries risk**. Decide both before recommending a product.

## 2. Default for general population

- **Under 3 years:** at least **1,000ppm**, smear only
- **3 to 6 years:** at least **1,000ppm**, pea-sized
- **7 years and over (children and adults):** **1,350 to 1,500ppm** (standard family toothpaste)

## 3. Higher caries risk: step up to family strength early

- For children **under 7 at higher risk**, use **1,350 to 1,500ppm** instead of 1,000ppm — *unless* the child cannot be prevented from eating toothpaste
- Maximum over-the-counter strength in the UK is **1,500ppm**

## 4. Prescription-only higher concentrations

For active caries despite standard prevention, prescribe higher-dose toothpaste. The age thresholds matter.

### Sodium fluoride 2,800ppm
- **Indication:** high caries risk patients aged **10 years and over** with caries present, cariogenic diet or cariogenic medication
- Use as a short-term risk-reduction measure while sugar intake is reduced

### Sodium fluoride 5,000ppm
- **Indication:** high caries risk patients aged **16 years and over**
- Particularly for: root or coronal caries, dry mouth, overdentures, cariogenic diet or medication, post head and neck radiotherapy or chemotherapy

## 5. Application instructions for high-strength paste

- 2cm ribbon on toothbrush head, **3 times daily**
- Spit out excess; do not rinse
- Adults with limited capacity need carer support to ensure correct amount used

## 6. Review

Review at routine oral health assessments. Continue high-fluoride paste only for those who cannot reduce caries susceptibility.

workflows.title: Applying fluoride varnish in practice
workflows.overview:
## 1. Confirm indication

Fluoride varnish (sodium fluoride **22,600ppm / 2.26% NaF**) is one of the strongest topical caries-prevention tools and is a strong recommendation in DBOH.

- **All children 3 to 17 years:** apply **2x/year** as part of general prevention
- **Higher caries risk (any age):** apply **2 or more** times per year
- **Higher-risk under 3:** also 2 or more times per year
- Increasingly indicated in **frail older adults** with retained natural teeth

## 2. Screen for contraindications

Before applying, check medical history for:

- **Ulcerative gingivitis or stomatitis** — contraindicated
- **Severe asthma** requiring hospitalisation — contraindicated for colophony-containing varnish
- **Severe allergy** (in particular to sticking plaster, which signals colophony allergy) — contraindicated for colophony-containing varnish

Some varnishes use other resins; check the specific product's SPC.

## 3. Prepare the teeth

1. Take consent and explain procedure
2. Remove gross plaque (full prophy is **not** essential)
3. Dry teeth

## 4. Apply

1. Apply thin layer to all teeth, focusing on susceptible sites (occlusal pits, smooth surfaces, exposed roots in adults)
2. Allow to set on saliva contact
3. Trained dental nurses can apply on prescription of a dentist

## 5. Aftercare

- Soft food only and avoid brushing for the rest of the day
- Avoid hot drinks for several hours

## 6. Notes on Muslim patients and alcohol

Fluoride varnishes containing alcohol are agreed as suitable for Muslim patients (West Midlands Shari'ah Council) provided used in small medicinal amounts and not for vanity reasons.

## 7. Off-licence prescribing

Many varnishes on the market are not licensed specifically for caries control. Apply professional responsibility for off-licence use and act in the patient's best interest.

workflows.title: Very Brief Advice (VBA) on smoking
workflows.overview:
## 1. Ask

At every contact, establish the patient's smoking status and **record** it.

Use plain prompts:

- *Do you smoke?*
- *Do you use tobacco products such as snuff, paan, chewing tobacco, or shisha?*
- *Have you ever smoked or used tobacco in the past? When did you stop?*

Record status as **smoker / ex-smoker / never smoker**.

## 2. Examine for tobacco signs

Alongside oral cancer screening and BPE, look for:

- Staining
- Halitosis
- Mucosal changes
- Periodontal breakdown

## 3. Advise (without asking permission first)

Do **not** ask *Do you want to quit?* — it triggers defensiveness. Instead, make a single statement:

> *Research shows the best way to stop is with a combination of specialist support and medication. You are up to 4 times as likely to quit with assistance. I can help arrange both of these.*

Key factual content the patient should hear:

- Combination behavioural support plus pharmacotherapy is the most effective approach
- **Combination NRT** (a patch plus a fast-acting form like gum) and **varenicline** are equally effective first-line
- **E-cigarettes** are far less harmful than smoking and are an effective quit aid
- Bupropion is an alternative

## 4. Act on the response

### If the patient is interested
- Refer to local stop smoking service (active referral, not signpost)
- Recommend NRT (patches, gum, inhalator, lozenges, nasal spray)
- Acknowledge e-cigarettes as a recognised quit aid
- Record in clinical notes

### If the patient is not interested
- Use a face-saving line: *That's fine, but help is available. Let me know if you change your mind.*
- Record advice given and patient response
- Re-ask at the next visit — VBA often takes multiple rounds before a quit attempt

## 5. Smokeless tobacco

For paan, gutkha, naswar, snus and similar products, follow the same Ask-Advise-Act pathway. Use product images if names are unfamiliar. Refer to specialist services where available.

## 6. Ex-smokers

People who have completely switched to vaping are recorded as **non-smokers** in dental records.

workflows.title: Alcohol Identification and Brief Advice using AUDIT-C
workflows.overview:
## 1. Ask: complete AUDIT-C

AUDIT-C is a 3-question screen, scored 0–12. The questions are:

1. **How often** do you have a drink containing alcohol?
2. How many **units** do you drink on a typical day when you are drinking?
3. **How often** do you have 6+ units (women) or 8+ units (men) on a single occasion?

Each answer scores 0 to 4. A scratch card can be used for self-completion.

## 2. Score and interpret

### Score 0 to 4: low risk
- Give **positive feedback**
- Encourage them to keep their drinking at low-risk levels

### Score 5 to 10: increasing or higher risk
- Give **brief advice**: highlight risks of alcohol harm including cancers of the mouth, throat and breast
- Reinforce CMO low-risk guidance:
  - **Not regularly more than 14 units per week**
  - Spread over 3 or more days
  - Have several drink-free days
- Provide a leaflet

### Score 11 or 12: probable dependence
- **Refer** to GP or community specialist alcohol service
- Do **not** simply tell them to stop — withdrawal can be dangerous and may need medically supervised detox

## 3. Tailor for special groups

### Pregnant or planning pregnancy
- The safest approach is **no alcohol**

### Combined tobacco and alcohol
- Both can be discussed in one session
- Let the patient choose which to tackle first
- A few units of alcohol can undermine willpower for smoking cessation, so flag this if they are quitting tobacco

## 4. Document

Record AUDIT-C score, advice given, and patient response in the clinical notes.

workflows.title: Oral cancer detection and urgent referral pathway
workflows.overview:
## 1. Ask (all patients)

- Update medical, social and dental history
- Explore tobacco use (chapter 11 pathway)
- Use AUDIT-C for alcohol
- Record advice given and patient response in clinical notes

## 2. Examine (all patients)

At every oral health assessment perform conventional visual and tactile examination.

### Extraoral
- Lips
- Neck
- Lymph nodes

### Intraoral
- All soft tissues, visual and tactile

Do **not** rely on vital staining, oral cytology, light-based detection or oral spectroscopy for evaluating lesions.

## 3. Recognise high-risk symptoms

**Refer urgently (2-week wait / suspected cancer pathway)** for any of:

- Unexplained ulceration in the oral cavity lasting **>3 weeks**
- Persistent unexplained lump in the neck
- Lump on the lip or in the oral cavity consistent with oral cancer
- Red patch (erythroplakia)
- Red and white patch (erythroleukoplakia / speckled leukoplakia)
- Persistent unexplained hoarseness
- Persistent throat pain or pain on swallowing **>3 weeks**

Less common but important:

- Unexplained tooth mobility unrelated to periodontitis
- Delayed extraction socket healing
- Fixed lesion
- Regional lymphadenopathy
- Dysphagia, weight loss, cranial neuropathies

## 4. High-risk patients (tobacco, alcohol, betel quid, prior lesion)

### Advise
Share modifiable risk factor approaches per chapter 11 (tobacco) and 12 (alcohol).

### Act
- For interested patients: refer to stop smoking support, GP or pharmacist; provide leaflets; consider GP/specialist alcohol referral if AUDIT-C is high
- For uninterested: *That's fine, but help is available. Let me know if you change your mind.* Re-ask at next visit

## 5. Refer

Use the **urgent suspected cancer (2-week-wait)** pathway via local head and neck cancer policy. The diagnostic gold standard is **scalpel biopsy with histology** carried out by the specialist team.

## 6. After cancer treatment

Patients who have had radiotherapy or chemotherapy to head and neck remain at high risk of:

- Caries
- Mucositis
- Osteoradionecrosis
- Periodontitis and peri-implantitis
- Reduced salivary flow and limited mouth opening

Intensify preventive care lifelong.

workflows.title: BPE-driven periodontal management for adults
workflows.overview:
## 1. Screen with BPE

Use the WHO BPE probe and code each sextant.

| Code | Observation |
|---|---|
| 0 | Healthy, no bleeding on probing |
| 1 | Bleeding on probing |
| 2 | Plaque retention factor (calculus, overhang) |
| 3 | Pocket 4 to 5.5mm (black band partially obscured) |
| 4 | Pocket 6mm or greater (black band completely obscured) |
| * | Furcation involvement |

For children:
- **7 to 11 years:** index teeth, codes 0–2 only
- **12 to 17 years:** index teeth, full codes

## 2. Manage by code

### Code 0 or 1
- Risk factor control (plaque, smoking, diabetes, medications)
- Recall as low-risk

### Code 2
- **Remove the retention factor** (calculus, overhang)
- Risk factor control

### Code 3
- Risk factor control + remove retention factors
- **6-point pocket chart** in the affected sextant
- Detailed assessment with radiographs, classification and grading (2017 BSP)
- Active treatment (initial therapy: OHI + PMPR)
- Re-evaluate response, then move to supportive periodontal care (SPC)

### Code 4 (or *)
- All of code 3 *plus* **full-mouth 6-point pocket chart**
- Full radiographic and staging assessment
- Stepwise therapy per BSP S3 guideline
- SPC for life

## 3. Stepwise therapy (after diagnosis)

1. **Behaviour change and self-care** — OHI, interdental cleaning, smoking cessation, diabetes optimisation
2. **Subgingival instrumentation** — PMPR for pockets ≥4mm with bleeding
3. **Reassessment** — at 3 months
4. **Refer / advanced therapy** if residual deep pockets
5. **Supportive periodontal care** — long-term maintenance

## 4. Stage and grade

Stage I to IV by interproximal bone loss (coronal third → apical third). Grade A to C by % bone loss / age (<0.5 / 0.5–1.0 / >1.0).

## 5. Risk factor control (table 2d)

- **Tobacco:** ask, advise, act (VBA)
- **Diabetes:** explain risk; ask HbA1c; aim <7.0% / 48 mmol/mol; liaise with physician
- **Medications:** check for dry mouth or gingival enlargement; consider physician letter for substitution
- **Plaque retention factors:** restoration overhangs, supra/subgingival calculus

workflows.title: Periodontal management for the diabetic patient
workflows.overview:
## 1. Establish diabetes context

People with diabetes are at greater risk of periodontitis and respond less well to therapy when poorly controlled. Hyperglycaemia in those without a diagnosis is also a risk factor.

- **Assume increased perio risk for anyone with diabetes**, even if currently well-controlled
- Confirm type 1, type 2, or pre-diabetic

## 2. Ask about glycaemic control

Ask the patient (or their physician):

- Most recent **HbA1c**
- Target HbA1c set by their team

### Target values
- **<7.0% (8.6 mmol/L)** = good control
- **6.5% / 48 mmol/mol** is the typical IFCC / DCCT target

Note that units may be % or mmol/mol depending on the patient's team.

## 3. Explain the bidirectional link

- Diabetes worsens periodontitis (hyperglycaemia impairs response to treatment)
- Periodontitis can worsen glycaemic control
- Periodontal therapy may improve diabetes control and reduce complications

## 4. Examine and screen

- Standard BPE
- Look for additional signs of poor diabetes control: dry mouth, mucosal candidiasis, slow healing

## 5. Manage perio in the usual stepwise way (BPE-driven)

Apply the standard BPE-driven pathway *plus*:

- Reinforce diet, medication, exercise and follow-up with the diabetes team
- Consider shorter recall
- **Write to the patient's diabetes physician** to share periodontal status — a downloadable template letter is published with DBOH
- Ask the physician for guidance on HbA1c level

## 6. Document and follow up

- HbA1c, source (patient or physician), date
- Periodontal diagnosis communicated to physician
- Reassess perio response after stepwise therapy at 3 months

## 7. Re-evaluate

If perio fails to respond as expected, suspect ongoing poor glycaemic control and re-engage with the medical team.

workflows.title: Dietary advice to reduce caries risk
workflows.overview:
## 1. Establish the rule

Caries risk is driven by **frequency** and **amount** of free sugars. Stephan curve: every sugar exposure drops biofilm pH for 20–40 minutes; repeated exposures keep pH below the demineralisation threshold.

**Free sugars** (SACN definition) include all sugars added by manufacturer/cook/consumer, plus those in honey, syrups, smoothies and fruit juices. They exclude sugars in whole fresh fruit and milk.

## 2. Set the headline message

- **Minimise the amount and frequency** of sugar-containing foods and drinks
- **Avoid sugar at bedtime** when salivary flow drops and buffering capacity is reduced
- All sugary food and drink should be **with meals**, not as snacks
- Free sugars: target **<5% of total energy intake** (SACN)

## 3. Concrete daily limits (children)

| Age | Max free sugar per day |
|---|---|
| 4 to 6 | 19g (~5 cubes) |
| 7 to 10 | 24g (~6 cubes) |
| 11+ | 30g (~7 cubes) |

One cube ≈ 4g.

## 4. Watch out for hidden free sugars

- Honey, fruit smoothies, fresh fruit juice, dried fruit — all cariogenic
- Fruit juice / smoothies: limit combined to **150ml per day** with meals
- Soft drinks, fruit drinks, squashes — *no place* in a child's daily diet
- Cereals, sauces, baby finger foods, baby "pouches"

## 5. Diet history when intervening

For higher-risk patients, take a structured diet history:

1. Total intakes per day (food and drink)
2. Number containing sugar
3. Number between meals
4. Any sugar before bedtime

An example diet diary is published with DBOH.

## 6. Replace, don't just remove

- **Sugar swap** drinks: water, lower-fat milk, sugar-free alternatives, tea, coffee
- Snack swaps: fresh fruit, frozen fruit, fruit canned in juice, vegetables
- Use the **Eatwell Guide** (does not apply under 2 years; partial application 2–5 years)

## 7. Special situations

### Long-term liquid medications
- Check BNF for sugar-free version
- Write to GP requesting prescription change
- If no sugar-free version, advise taking with meals where possible; intensify fluoride

### Older adults / care homes
- Polypharmacy → xerostomia → caries risk
- Sugary oral nutritional supplements common
- Often impractical to remove — focus on fluoride

### Babies and toddlers
- No added sugar to food or drinks
- Bottle: only breast milk, formula or cooled boiled water
- Free-flow cup from 6 months; discourage bottle from 1 year
- Sugar-free medicines

## 8. Behaviour change framing

Use SMART goals (chapter 3). One change at a time. Recognise that fear, cost and habit are barriers, especially in deprived populations.

workflows.title: Tooth wear assessment and management with BEWE
workflows.overview:
## 1. Screen with BEWE at every routine examination

The Basic Erosive Wear Examination scores the **most severely affected surface in each sextant** on a 4-point scale.

| Score | Description |
|---|---|
| 0 | No erosive wear |
| 1 | Initial loss of surface texture ("frosted glass") |
| 2 | Distinct defect, hard tissue loss <50% of surface; dentine often involved |
| 3 | Hard tissue loss >50% of surface |

Sum the sextant scores → cumulative score guides management. **A score of 3 in every sextant** signals severe wear needing further investigation.

## 2. Decide if wear is age-related or accelerated

Most wear is gradual and physiological. "Accelerated tooth wear" is the indication for active intervention. Look for a mismatch between wear and patient age.

## 3. For general population (no accelerated wear)

- Standard oral health advice (caries + perio)
- Standard fluoride toothpaste, twice daily, spit not rinse
- Eatwell Guide diet, including fruit and vegetables
- Limit fruit juice / smoothies to 150ml/day
- Sugar-sweetened (especially carbonated) drinks: avoid or minimise
- **Do not** discourage fruit consumption — most people don't eat enough

## 4. For accelerated wear: identify the source

Wear is multifactorial. Investigate three categories.

### Extrinsic acid (chemical)
- **Drinks:** carbonated, wine, alcopops, fortified wines, smoothies, energy drinks, citric-acid drinks (orange, lemon, blackcurrant), fruit teas, sports drinks
- **Foods:** vinegar-based, fruit-based sauces, acidic sweets
- **Fruit:** mainly a risk in high quantity; *do not* discourage unless identified as the cause
- **Medication:** chewable vitamin C, aspirin, asthma inhalers, iron preparations
- **Workplace:** acid mists, swimming pools, wine tasting
- **Whitening materials**

### Intrinsic acid
- GORD, laryngopharyngeal reflux
- Chronic vomiting in pregnancy
- Eating disorders
- Rumination

### Mechanical
- Aggressive brushing
- High-abrasive toothpaste
- Bruxism
- Object-opening with teeth, piercings, occupational particulates

## 5. Manage the identified risk

### Diet
- Reduce frequency of identified acidic intake
- Keep acidic items to mealtimes
- Avoid swilling, swishing, holding in mouth
- Substitute with plain water, milk, tea, coffee

### Brushing
- Age-appropriate fluoride toothpaste twice daily
- Avoid high-abrasive paste
- Consider stannous fluoride paste
- Timing of brushing not critical (no need to delay routinely after meals)

### Vomiting (any cause)
- **Do not brush after vomiting** — rinse with water
- Apply fluoride toothpaste with finger, or use fluoride mouthrinse

### Intrinsic causes
- Refer to GP for reflux or eating disorders

### Saliva
- Identify medications that suppress flow
- Saliva substitutes if needed

## 6. Monitor

- Repeat BEWE
- Photographs and study casts for severe cases
- Consider shortened recall
- Intra-oral scans emerging as monitoring tools

firstPrinciples.title: Caries is driven by dietary sugar feeding biofilm bacteria
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Dental caries is one of the commonest non-communicable diseases globally and the chief driver of oral pain in children, yet it is largely preventable.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Sugar, biofilm, acid

Dental caries is caused by dietary sugars broken down by the biofilm on the tooth surface, which produces acids that demineralise enamel over time [1]. Without dietary sugar, the cariogenic biofilm cannot generate the acid needed to dissolve the tooth.

## Why frequency matters more than amount

The Stephan curve shows that biofilm pH falls within a minute of a sugar exposure and takes 20 to 40 minutes to recover through saliva buffering. If sugar exposures cluster, the pH stays below the demineralisation threshold and the tooth loses mineral faster than it can be replaced [2]. This is why the clinical message is to minimise both the amount and the frequency of free sugars, not just the total.

## Practical implication

If the patient cannot reduce their sugar intake, every other intervention (fluoride, varnish, sealants) is essentially trying to compensate for the same underlying driver. The first lever to pull, when prevention isn't working, is dietary sugar.

citations.quote: The disease is caused by dietary sugars that are broken down by micro-organisms in the biofilm on a tooth surface, which produces acids that, over time, demineralise tooth enamel.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 4: dental caries

citations.quote: When sugar intakes are spaced some hours apart, there is a good opportunity for remineralisation, which is also more effective in the presence of fluoride.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 10: healthier eating

firstPrinciples.title: Caries is reversible until the surface breaks down
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The dynamic balance between demineralisation and remineralisation defines whether a lesion progresses, arrests or reverses, and is the basis for all preventive caries management.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A dynamic process

Demineralisation and remineralisation alternate continuously. In the early stages, caries can be reversed; once factors promoting demineralisation outweigh those favouring remineralisation, the lesion progresses into dentine and ultimately cavitates [1].

## Implication for clinical decision-making

A pre-cavitation lesion is not a restorative problem — it is a balance problem. Tip the balance back by reducing sugar exposure and increasing fluoride availability and the lesion can heal. This is the rationale behind the ICCMS approach and behind the entire fluoride-and-diet emphasis of DBOH.

## Why cavitation is the watershed

Once the surface breaks, mechanical plaque removal and remineralisation can no longer reach the lesion floor. After that point, restoration becomes necessary. Catching lesions before this transition is the single highest-yield clinical activity in caries management.

citations.quote: In the early stages of the disease, dental caries can be reversed. However, when factors promoting demineralisation exceed those favouring remineralisation, dental caries progresses (unless checked) into dentine to a point where the tooth surface breaks down and ultimately a cavity forms.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 4: dental caries

firstPrinciples.title: Fluoride works topically by shifting the demineralisation balance
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Decades of decline in childhood caries are attributed to fluoride toothpaste, the single most important public-health intervention against dental caries.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Where fluoride acts

Fluoride acts topically. Regular exposure maintains a concentration in the plaque biofilm that encourages remineralisation of the tooth surface and inhibits the cariogenic bacteria's acid production [1]. The benefit is not from systemic ingestion at toothbrushing-relevant doses; it is from sustained low-level presence in the oral environment.

## Concentration and frequency both matter

Higher fluoride concentrations in toothpaste produce better caries control [2], and brushing twice rather than once daily lowers caries risk by about 14%. Spitting rather than rinsing after brushing keeps the topical effect going longer.

## Why this changes practice

The "don't rinse" rule is not a quirk; it follows directly from the topical mechanism. So does the rationale for fluoride varnish, mouthrinse, and high-strength toothpaste — all are ways to keep more fluoride in the biofilm for longer.

citations.quote: Regular exposure to fluoride maintains a concentration in the plaque biofilm that encourages remineralisation of the tooth surface.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 9: fluoride

citations.quote: Higher concentration of fluoride in toothpaste leads to better caries control.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 8: oral hygiene

firstPrinciples.title: Saliva is the natural defence against acid attack
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Saliva buffers acids, clears debris, delivers calcium, phosphate and fluoride for remineralisation, and falls dramatically during sleep.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Buffering and clearance

Saliva production rises at mealtimes and is much reduced during sleep. The buffering action of saliva returns biofilm pH to normal over 20 to 40 minutes after a sugar exposure [1]. In the same period it clears food debris and delivers calcium and phosphate to the tooth surface.

## Why bedtime sugar is the worst time

When salivary flow drops at night, both the buffering and the clearance disappear. Sugar consumed at bedtime stays in contact with the teeth for hours rather than minutes — hence the universal advice to avoid sugar at bedtime [2].

## Xerostomia in older adults

Reduced salivary flow from polypharmacy, head and neck radiotherapy or systemic disease shifts the demineralisation balance unfavourably. This is why dry-mouth older adults are flagged as caries-risk and prescribed high-strength fluoride paste irrespective of diet.

citations.quote: This process stops as the buffering action of saliva returns the pH to normal (20 to 40 minutes). Saliva production varies across a 24-hour day, being stimulated at mealtimes whereas it is much reduced during sleep.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 10: healthier eating

citations.quote: Avoid sugar-containing foods and drinks at bedtime when saliva flow is reduced and buffering capacity is lost.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 2: summary guidance tables

firstPrinciples.title: Periodontitis is plaque-initiated but host-mediated
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Periodontitis affects almost half of UK adults and causes most adult tooth loss, but susceptibility varies and the destruction is driven by the immune response, not the bacteria directly.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Dysbiosis triggers an immune attack

Dental plaque is a structured biofilm. Small amounts cause minimal inflammation, but a disruption of the balance — dysbiosis — between plaque and the host's immune system initiates gingivitis and can progress to periodontitis [1]. Most of the tissue destruction is caused by the host's own inflammatory response rather than direct bacterial cytotoxicity.

## Plaque is necessary but not sufficient

Gingivitis is reversible by reducing plaque [2]. Not everyone with gingivitis develops periodontitis — susceptibility is shaped by smoking, diabetes, genetics and other modifiers. So plaque control prevents the trigger, but susceptibility determines whether the trigger leads to attachment loss.

## Bone loss is irreversible

While gingival inflammation reverses, bone loss in periodontitis is essentially permanent. This is why early detection and lifelong supportive care matter, and why staging captures historical bone loss while grading captures the speed of breakdown.

citations.quote: Normally, small amounts of bacteria cause only minimal inflammation, but a disruption in the balance (dysbiosis) between the plaque and the person's immune system can lead to the initiation of gingivitis and progression to periodontitis.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 5: periodontal diseases

citations.quote: Such inflammation is reversible by reducing levels of dental plaque at and below the gingival margin.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 5: periodontal diseases

firstPrinciples.title: Smoking is the single largest modifiable risk factor for periodontitis
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Tobacco roughly doubles the risk of periodontal breakdown, masks bleeding signs, and impairs the response to treatment, making it the single change with the largest perio impact.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Direct and indirect harm

Tobacco smoking and smokeless tobacco have a profound effect on the risk of developing periodontitis and impair treatment response [1]. Nicotine reduces gingival blood flow, blunts bleeding (a key clinical sign), and shifts the inflammatory response toward more destruction. Smoking also enriches periodontopathic species.

## Cessation reverses some harm

Cessation prevents further deterioration of periodontal health [1]. The improvement is not retroactive — lost bone does not return — but the rate of breakdown drops back toward never-smoker levels.

## Why this dominates clinical priorities

No other single modifiable factor in periodontal care comes close. For a smoker with periodontitis, smoking cessation will achieve more than any non-surgical or surgical therapy alone, which is why VBA on smoking is embedded in every BPE-driven pathway.

citations.quote: Tobacco smoking and use of smokeless tobacco products have a profound effect on the risk of developing periodontitis. They also impair the treatment response. Cessation of tobacco use can prevent further deterioration of periodontal health.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 5: periodontal diseases

firstPrinciples.title: Diabetes and periodontitis are bidirectionally linked
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Hyperglycaemia worsens periodontitis and periodontitis worsens glycaemic control, and treatment of one can improve the other.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why hyperglycaemia worsens perio

Glycaemia in those without diabetes, and hyperglycaemia in those with diabetes, are both risk factors for poor periodontal health and impair treatment response [1]. Advanced glycation end-products and hyperglycaemia-driven inflammation amplify the host response to plaque, accelerating attachment loss.

## Why perio worsens diabetes

The systemic inflammatory load from periodontitis raises insulin resistance. International consensus is that periodontal therapy reduces the risks of diabetes and its complications [2], and periodontal treatment improves metabolic control in type 2 diabetes (moderate certainty).

## Practical clinical move

For a diabetic patient with periodontitis, asking about HbA1c, writing to the diabetes physician with the periodontal status, and aiming for HbA1c below 7.0% (or 48 mmol/mol) are all part of treatment, not optional extras.

citations.quote: Glycaemia in those without a diagnosis of diabetes, and hyperglycaemia in those with diabetes are both risk factors for poor periodontal health and also impair the response to its treatment.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 5: periodontal diseases

citations.quote: International consensus of joint dental and medical experts, based on evidence from systematic reviews, recommends the importance of periodontal therapy in reducing the risks of diabetes and its complications.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 5: periodontal diseases

firstPrinciples.title: Tobacco and alcohol multiply each other's oral cancer risk
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Tobacco and alcohol are independent risk factors for oral cancer, but their combined risk is multiplicative, and both have no safe lower limit.
firstPrinciples.body:
## No safe lower limit

Compared with zero use, the risks of mouth and oropharyngeal cancer increase with any level of tobacco or alcohol [1]. There is no level of regular alcohol consumption that improves oral health.

## Multiplicative interaction

Using both tobacco and alcohol increases oral cancer risk exponentially. People who drink and smoke heavily have an over 10-fold increased risk compared with those who abstain from both [2]. The two behaviours also cluster — about a quarter of smokers drink above low-risk guidelines.

## Different exposure patterns matter for each

For smoking, **duration** is more important than frequency — fewer cigarettes over many years carries more risk than many cigarettes over fewer years. For alcohol, **frequency** is more important than duration — heavy intake over a few years outweighs light intake over many. This shapes how questions are asked and what kinds of changes are recommended.

citations.quote: Compared with zero tobacco use and alcohol consumption, the risks of mouth and oropharyngeal cancer increase with any level of tobacco use or alcohol consumption - there are no safe lower limits.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 6: oral cancer

citations.quote: It is estimated that people who both drink and smoke heavily have an over 10-fold increased risk of developing oral cancer than those people who abstain from both products.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 6: oral cancer

firstPrinciples.title: Oral cancer survival depends overwhelmingly on stage at diagnosis
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Five-year survival from mouth cancer is around 56% overall, but rises sharply with earlier diagnosis, putting clinical visual examination at the centre of prognosis.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Stage drives prognosis

Oral cancer survival rates are strongly associated with the stage at diagnosis [1]. Just over half of people diagnosed with mouth cancer in England between 2009 and 2013 survived five years; the figure rises substantially when caught early.

## Conventional examination is the screening test

Most symptomless mouth cancers can be detected by visual examination by clinicians. Adjuncts like vital staining, oral cytology and light-based detection are *not* recommended for evaluating suspicious lesions [2]. The gold standard for diagnosis is scalpel biopsy with histology by the specialist team.

## Why dentists hold the key

Dentists and dental team members are the only professionals who routinely examine a patient's mouth. The structured visual and tactile examination at every check, combined with knowing the urgent referral triggers (>3-week ulcer, erythroplakia, persistent neck lump, hoarseness, dysphagia), is the most realistic system for early detection in the population.

citations.quote: Oral cancer survival rates are strongly associated with the stage at diagnosis. Early detection is key to improving oral cancer survival rates and quality of life.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 2: summary guidance tables

citations.quote: It's not recommended to use vital staining, oral cytology or light-based detection and/or oral spectroscopy for evaluating lesions for malignancy.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 2: summary guidance tables

firstPrinciples.title: HPV is now a major driver of oropharyngeal cancer
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Oropharyngeal cancer rates are rising rapidly across the UK, partly driven by oral HPV infection, with implications that extend beyond traditional tobacco-and-alcohol risk profiles.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A different epidemic

Oral HPV infection is a major risk factor for oropharyngeal cancer [1], and oropharyngeal cancer incidence is rising in all four UK nations — reportedly the fastest-rising incidence of any cancer in Scotland. HPV-related cancers tend to occur at a younger age and may have different prognostic features from classic tobacco-and-alcohol oropharyngeal cancers.

## Why the dental team should know

Unlike traditional risk factors, HPV is not modifiable through brief advice in the chair. The strongest preventive lever is vaccination of young people, both boys and girls. Awareness of the changing epidemiology means the team should not assume oropharyngeal symptoms in a non-smoker are low-risk.

## Implication for examination

Persistent symptoms in the throat — hoarseness over 3 weeks, pain on swallowing over 3 weeks, persistent neck lumps — must trigger an urgent referral irrespective of the patient's tobacco and alcohol history.

citations.quote: Oral HPV infection is a major risk factor for oropharyngeal cancer in particular.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 6: oral cancer

firstPrinciples.title: Tooth wear is multifactorial with no single critical pH
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Unlike caries, dental erosion does not have a clean threshold below which tooth surface dissolves; calcium content, salivary flow and contact time all moderate the risk.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why erosion is different from caries

Unlike demineralisation in dental caries, there is no clear-cut critical pH for dental erosion to occur, because other influences such as a drink's mineral content moderate its erosive action [1]. Calcium-enriched drinks may be less erosive than their pH alone would suggest, and saliva plays a crucial role in dilution, buffering and clearance of acids.

## What raises erosive potential

Lower pH, lower salivary flow, lower buffering capacity, higher titratable acidity, lower calcium and phosphate, lower fluoride, and higher temperature all increase erosion. Drinking habits matter as much as the drink itself: swilling, swishing or holding acidic drinks in the mouth prolongs contact and overwhelms saliva.

## Implication for management

Tooth wear management is rarely about banning a single food. It's about identifying the dominant risk factor (extrinsic acid, intrinsic acid, mechanical) for that patient and reducing frequency and contact time. Restricting fruit, in particular, should not be advised unless fruit is specifically identified as the cause.

citations.quote: Unlike demineralisation in dental caries, there is no clear-cut critical pH for dental erosion to occur, because other influences such as a drink's mineral content may moderate its erosive action.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 7: tooth wear

firstPrinciples.title: Plaque is necessary for periodontitis but susceptibility decides the outcome
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Identical plaque levels produce gingivitis in everyone but periodontitis in only some people, because attachment loss depends on host factors as much as on the biofilm.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Plaque alone doesn't explain it

Gingivitis and periodontitis are separate conditions, although both are initiated by plaque in susceptible people [1]. Gingivitis is a risk factor for periodontitis but not all gingivitis progresses. The clinical implication is that good plaque control prevents the trigger but doesn't override individual susceptibility entirely.

## Routine scale and polish has no clinical benefit in healthy patients

No clinical benefits of routine scale and polish have been demonstrated for adults with good periodontal health [2]. The benefit of professional intervention is concentrated in patients with established disease who need PMPR plus self-care reinforcement.

## Where the leverage is

In primary prevention the lever is the patient's own daily plaque removal, supported by behaviour change. In secondary and tertiary prevention the lever is risk-factor control plus targeted PMPR — not routine scaling for everyone.

citations.quote: Gingivitis and periodontitis are separate conditions, although both are initiated by plaque in susceptible people.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 5: periodontal diseases

citations.quote: No clinical benefits of 'routine scale and polish' have been demonstrated for adults with good periodontal health.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 5: periodontal diseases

firstPrinciples.title: Behaviour change requires capability, opportunity and motivation
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Most preventive dentistry depends on patients changing daily habits, but information alone rarely changes behaviour; the COM-B framework explains why.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The COM-B model

For behaviour change to occur, a person must have the **capability**, **opportunity** and **motivation** to change [1]. Capability is the physical or psychological ability and skill. Opportunity is the social and physical environment. Motivation is the internal drive, including habit and emotional response.

## Why information alone fails

The provision of health information may increase knowledge, but it will not achieve sustained behaviour change for most people. Many patients fully understand the consequences of their behaviour and still struggle to change — the problem is not information but capability or opportunity or motivation.

## Practical use

When a patient is not changing, the question is *which of the three is missing?* A homeless smoker with stress-driven cigarette use has an opportunity problem. A child without parental supervision at brushing has a capability problem. A patient who doesn't believe smoking damages oral health has a motivation problem. Each has a different intervention.

citations.quote: This model proposes that for behaviour change to occur, a person must have the capability, opportunity and motivation to change behaviour.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 3: behaviour change

firstPrinciples.title: Brief structured advice doubles smoking quit rates
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Very Brief Advice from a healthcare professional, taking under a minute, materially raises a smoker's chance of quitting, especially when paired with pharmacotherapy.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The numbers

Research suggests 95% of patients expect to be asked about smoking, and a short intervention can make all the difference [1]. People are 3 times as likely to quit successfully if they use a combination of stop-smoking aids together with specialist help and support [2]. Combination NRT and varenicline are the most effective first-line pharmacotherapies.

## Why the dental team is well-placed

Dental teams see large numbers of "healthy" patients in primary care. VBA takes about 30 seconds, follows the ask-advise-act structure, and avoids asking *do you want to quit?* — which triggers defensiveness. Instead, advice is delivered as a single statement and the patient is offered referral.

## Many rounds, eventual change

Most smokers need VBA on multiple occasions before they are ready to act. Re-asking at each visit is part of the protocol, not a failure of the previous attempt.

citations.quote: Research suggests that 95% of patients expect to be asked about smoking and a short intervention can make all the difference.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 11: smoking and tobacco use

citations.quote: People are 3 times as likely to quit successfully if they use a combination of stop smoking aids (including e-cigarettes) together with specialist help and support.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 11: smoking and tobacco use

firstPrinciples.title: Children's permanent incisors are at fluorosis risk only under age 3
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Fluoride exposure is calibrated by age because tooth crowns finish calcifying at predictable times, and the aesthetic risk window for permanent incisors is narrow.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The biology of the window

The risks of fluorosis damaging the appearance of permanent incisors are relevant only to ingestion of fluoride by those under 3 years old, because calcification of the crowns of permanent incisors is complete by 30 months [1]. For premolars, the risk window extends to under 6 years.

## Why a smear, then a pea

Under 3, a smear of toothpaste contains 0.1ml of paste — only 0.1mg fluoride at 1,000ppm. From 3 to 6, a pea is 0.25ml — 0.25mg fluoride. For a 15kg child these doses are an order of magnitude below toxicity even if entirely swallowed [2]. The smear-then-pea progression is calibrated against fluorosis risk, not safety.

## After 6 years

Fluorosis of cosmetic concern is essentially no longer at issue, so family-strength toothpaste (1,350 to 1,500ppm) becomes the standard from age 7 onwards. This biology underpins the entire age-banded toothpaste recommendation.

citations.quote: The risks of fluorosis damaging the appearance of permanent incisors are relevant only to ingestion of fluoride by those under 3 years old, as calcification of the crowns of permanent incisor teeth is complete by 30 months.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 9: fluoride

citations.quote: Overall, this results in an absorbable fluoride dose of only 0.007 to 0.01mg per kilogram of body weight if swallowed, for a child weighing 15kg.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 9: fluoride

firstPrinciples.title: Risk-based recall, not fixed intervals, drives prevention
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: NICE guidance and DBOH align on tailoring recall length to individual risk rather than booking everyone at the same interval, with bone loss in periodontitis being irreversible reinforcing the case.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why fixed intervals don't work

There is no evidence that a specific dental recall interval influences caries development or progression [1]. Recall must therefore be matched to the patient's risk and preventive needs, not to convention.

## The DBOH/NICE bands

The shortest interval is 3 months for any patient. The maximum is 12 months for under-18s and 24 months for adults, in line with NICE CG19 [2]. Higher-risk patients sit at the shorter end; established low-risk patients at the longer end.

## Why this matters operationally

A 6-month recall is a clinical default rather than evidence-based. Defending an extended recall in a low-risk adult is justified by NICE; shortening recall in a higher-risk patient is mandatory. Reviewing risk at every recall, not just at the new patient exam, is part of the standard.

citations.quote: There is no evidence that a specific dental recall interval influences dental caries development or progression.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 4: dental caries

citations.quote: The shortest interval between oral health reviews for all patients should be 3 months, the longest interval between oral health reviews for patients younger than 18 years should be 12 months and for patients aged 18 years and older, 24 months.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 1: introduction

firstPrinciples.title: Sealants prevent and arrest occlusal caries when retained
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Pit-and-fissure sealants reduce occlusal caries on permanent molars in higher-risk children, but their effectiveness depends on proper placement and ongoing maintenance.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The evidence

Resin-based fissure sealants are effective in preventing and arresting dental caries for up to 48 months compared with unsealed teeth (moderate-certainty evidence) [1]. Glass-ionomer evidence is less clear-cut.

## Technique-sensitive

The placement of sealants is highly technique-sensitive — poor moisture control or operative technique compromises retention and therefore the entire benefit [2]. Sealants must be checked at every visit for wear, integrity and leakage, and re-sealed when necessary.

## Who should get them

In DBOH the recommendation is targeted: resin-based sealants on eruption of permanent molars in children judged at higher caries risk. The mesial of a first permanent molar may also be sealed when the deciduous molar has been lost. Sealants in low-risk children are not part of the routine recommendation.

citations.quote: When compared with unsealed teeth, there is moderate-certainty evidence that resin-based fissure sealants are effective in preventing and arresting dental caries for up to 48 months.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 4: dental caries

citations.quote: The placement of sealants is highly technique-sensitive, with poor operative technique and/or a challenging environment affecting the retention of the sealant and therefore its success.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 4: dental caries

firstPrinciples.title: Most preventable disease clusters in deprived populations
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Deprivation accounts for a substantial fraction of caries variation in 5-year-olds, and oral cancer is two to three times more common in the lowest socioeconomic groups, making prevention an inequalities issue.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The size of the gap

Around 41% of variation in dental caries among 5-year-olds in England is accounted for by deprivation [1]. Data from Scotland reveals wide socioeconomic inequalities in oral cancer incidence, with those in the lowest socioeconomic groups having a near 3-fold greater incidence than the highest [2].

## Why behaviours cluster

Multiple unhealthy behaviours — smoking, alcohol misuse, poor diet, irregular toothbrushing — cluster in the same groups, often in patients facing fear, cost, time pressure or unstable housing. Brief advice that ignores these constraints often fails.

## Implication for clinical conduct

The response is not to assume disengaged patients don't value oral health, but to work in small, sustainable changes that respect their context, while recognising that population-level interventions (water fluoridation, sugar regulation, school programmes) do most of the heavy lifting at the upstream end.

citations.quote: While some of the variation in disease levels can be accounted for by deprivation (around 41% among 5 year olds), it is not the only risk factor.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 4: dental caries

citations.quote: Data from Scotland reveals wide socioeconomic inequalities in the incidence of oral cancer with those from lowest socioeconomic groups having a near 3-fold greater incidence risk ratio than those from the highest socioeconomic groups.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 6: oral cancer

firstPrinciples.title: Nicotine is the addictive driver, but the harm comes from combustion
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Public misconceptions blame nicotine for smoking-related cancer, when in fact the carcinogenic and cardiotoxic load lies in tobacco combustion products; this distinction shapes harm-reduction practice.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The misconception

While nicotine is the addictive substance in cigarettes, it is relatively harmless [1]. Almost all the harm from smoking comes from the thousands of other chemicals in tobacco smoke. UK survey data show 4 in 10 smokers wrongly think nicotine causes most of the smoking-related cancer.

## Implication for NRT and e-cigarettes

Nicotine replacement therapy and e-cigarettes can deliver nicotine without combustion. They are not risk-free, but the available evidence places their harm well below cigarette smoking, and they substantially raise quit success rates. Recommending them is consistent with harm reduction.

## Practical message

Smokers who can't or won't quit completely benefit from switching, even partially, to a nicotine-only delivery system. Telling smokers nicotine itself is the killer is not only inaccurate, it discourages the very switching behaviour that reduces their cancer risk.

citations.quote: While nicotine is the addictive substance in cigarettes, it is relatively harmless.
citations.source: Delivering Better Oral Health, Chapter 11: smoking and tobacco use
